title: Permissions in a design critique tool
excerpt: Say what each person can do on the frame: view, comment, resolve, or upload. A client link should state its power and its expiry, and internal notes must be impossible to send by accident.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table, one seat with one kind of access.
caption: One seat, one screen, a clear idea of what this person may change. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which roles does a small critique need?
faqs.answer: Someone who uploads and invites, teammates who comment and resolve, commenters who cannot close notes, and viewers. Guests should be time-boxed to one file. Put the sentence for this person on the file, in one line, so they do not hunt for a control that is not there.

faqs.question: Should clients be able to resolve comments?
faqs.answer: Only if you mean approval to close the work. Otherwise let them reply and say that the team marks notes done. Upload and delete stay with the owner. Removed notes should leave a line that they were removed, not a hole in the history.

faqs.question: How should a client link behave?
faqs.answer: State what it grants, which version it opens, and when it ends, both on the share screen and on the file. Viewing should not be promotable to commenting by the person who holds the link. When it expires, name who to ask. Internal notes never belong on that link.

markdown:
Clear design critique tool permissions ux shows a small team what they can do on the screen, and why a control is unavailable. Hidden buttons feel like bugs. A resolve action that fails after someone has written the decision feels like one too.

The W3C's WCAG overview puts the guidelines under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A boundary on a review file has to be perceivable as text and understandable as a reason. The server may refuse the action. The canvas still has to explain it.

## Roles in a small critique

Name the roles as sentences. The designer owns the file and the versions. A teammate comments and may resolve notes on work they share. A founder or client comments, and may be asked to approve, without rearranging the file. A guest with the link can view, and comments only if you said they could. An outside studio, if you work with one, needs a seat that ends when the engagement ends.

A practical set for a small team:

- Owner: upload versions, invite, comment, resolve, and delete the file.
- Teammate: comment, reply, resolve on this review.
- Commenter: comment and reply, cannot resolve or upload.
- Viewer: see the frame and the notes, write nothing.
- Guest: a time-boxed viewer or commenter, one file, not the whole workspace.

If the team is four people and a client, do not invent a role matrix that needs a diagram. Use the sentences. Add a role when a real person is blocked or over-powered, not when a template offered eight seats.

Write the sentence on the file, in one line, for the person who is looking. "You can comment on this draft. You cannot replace it." That line does more than a settings page they will not open while they are in the review. Keep it short enough to sit above the frame without becoming a banner.

## Comment, resolve, upload

Commenting and resolving are different powers. A client who can resolve will close notes the team still needs, often by accident, because resolve looks like "I have read this." If clients should not resolve, show the notes as open, let them reply, and say why there is no resolve control. "The design team marks notes done." Hiding the control with no line makes them look for it. The line lets them stop looking.

Uploading a new version changes the object everyone is pointing at. Limit it to owners and the designers on the file. If a commenter cannot upload, do not show an upload button that errors. They had no reason to expect it, so it can be absent. The version name can still be visible. Seeing the draft is not the same as replacing it.

Deleting a comment, or editing someone else's, is rare and sharp. Authors can edit their own words. Owners can delete a note that leaked a secret or landed on the wrong file, and the event should remain as "removed by Riley," not as a hole with no history. Silent deletion is how a team loses trust in the record. A small team can handle a visible removal. They cannot handle a vanishing objection.

Approving a frame, if you offer approval, is a named permission, not a comment with a special emoji. Say who has it. "Sam can approve this review." If approval is a comment intent anyone can set, say that too, so nobody treats a stranger's "approve" as the company's yes. The word is too strong to leave implicit.

## Guests, clients, and the link

A link is a seat you handed out. Say what it grants, on the share screen and on the file the guest opens. "View the homepage draft, comments visible, link expires Friday." If they can comment, the composer should say their name will appear. If they have not set a name, ask for one before the first note, so the team is not reading three comments from "Guest."

Do not let a view link be promoted to comment by anyone who holds it. Promotion is an owner action. A viewer who wants to comment can be shown how to ask. "You can view. Ask Riley if you should comment." That is a complete design. A 403 after they have typed a paragraph is not.

Clients often need a narrower file than the team. Internal notes, unfinished branches, and the messy duplicate artboard should stay off the client link. The clean way is a review that contains only the frames you meant to show, not a filter the client can clear. If you do use a filter, a client who removes it should not suddenly see the internal frames. The permission is the set of frames, not a toggle in their local UI.

Expiry should speak. "This link ended on Friday. Ask Riley for a new one." Name a person when you know one. A naked forbidden page wastes the client's goodwill and creates a message to your team anyway. Write the page as if you were still hosting them.

## Mentions and who gets mail

Mentioning someone grants them nothing by itself, but it does send their eyes to the file. If they have no seat, the mention should fail in a sentence and keep the comment. "Jordan is not on this review. The note is saved. Invite them if they should see the frame." Do not auto-invite on mention. Auto-invite is how a client list grows to include a contractor who was only supposed to be asked a question in chat.

Notification settings are personal. The permission to mute a file is not the permission to leave the file. Say the difference. "You will not be mailed. You can still comment." A mute that also removes someone's pins from the canvas is a bug with a bell icon.

Public comments and internal comments, if both exist, need a visible mode in the composer, defaulting to the safer one for guests. A client should not have an "internal" mode at all. A teammate should see which mode they are in before they type, not after they send. The most expensive permissions bug in a critique tool is a frank note that the client can read. Make the mode a label the size of the commit button's attention, not a tiny toggle.

## When the engagement ends

Remove a guest, a client, or a studio seat on a date you chose. Comments they already left can stay, attributed, so the work still makes sense. Their ability to add more, to resolve, or to open a new version should end. Say that on the file the team still sees. "Case Studio can view until Friday." After Friday, "Case Studio's access ended. Their notes remain."

Transferring ownership of a file is closer to handing over the archive than to toggling a comment switch. Confirm it with the file's name and what moves: versions, unresolved notes, the live link. A dropdown of teammates is too casual for that act. One sentence, then the save.

If a person is both client and teammate on different files, the role is per file, and the first screen should say which one this file uses. A global role that leaks client limits into an internal file, or internal notes into a client file, is the failure mode to test. Open both files with the same person. Read the one-line permission on each. They should not match unless you meant them to.

## Build the reason next to the control

Test with the actual client, or with someone playing them who did not design the file. Ask them to approve, to upload, and to resolve. The first should be possible only if you meant it. The other two should explain themselves in the line above the frame, before a tap. If the client asks "is it broken?" the line is missing or too quiet. Move it. A permissions model that requires a kickoff to understand is the wrong model for a link you sent so they could review alone.

Design the view-only canvas, the comment-only composer, and the owner version control as three screens, not as one screen with mystery meat. In the build, check the role when the action runs, and render the reason when you omit or disable the control. Next.js, React, and TypeScript can share one definition of the role between the page and the action. Prisma and PostgreSQL can store the seat, the expiry, and the note so a removed guest cannot post through an old tab forever.

Hanabi designs and builds these boundaries in Figma first, because the sentence on the canvas is a design problem. The implementation should not invent a second sentence. Tailwind keeps view-only and comment modes quiet and distinct. A team should feel the file is theirs, not that they are being policed. The words can still be exact.

People who cannot see the frame they expected will search. [Search inside a design critique tool](/blog/search-inside-a-design-critique-tool) is the next piece, because search has to respect the same seats, and it has to explain a miss that is really a file they were never meant to open.

If you want to see how a small product shows a boundary without feeling broken, look through [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Notice where a screen says what you can do. That sentence is the permissions model your critique tool is missing.
